The VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) provides settlement functions for the BASE II System and Single Message System (SMS), including Interlink. Clients and processors get settlement information in a standardized set of reports using common business-oriented terminology. VSS provides flexibility in defining financial relationships, selecting reports and report destinations, and establishing funds transfer points. Visa processes interchange transactions for SMS (including Interlink) and BASE II through separate systems. SMS and BASE II perform their own clearing functions and VSS performs the settlement functions for SMS and BASE II.

Clearing is the process of collecting an individual transaction from one client or processor and delivering it to another. Settlement is the process of calculating and determining the net financial position of each client for all transactions that are cleared.
This figure shows the VSS clearing and settlement process.
Visa offers several settlement services options.

International Settlement Service – Used to settle all international transactions and domestic transactions for clients that do not participate in a National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) or Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS). National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) – Allows clients within a country to settle qualifying domestic transactions through a central settlement agent bank. Qualifying transactions are those in which the merchant, acquirer, and issuer are in the same country. Also, the transaction currency must be the local currency for that country for the transaction to qualify. Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS) – Allows clients within a defined area to settle qualifying domestic transactions through a central settlement agent bank. Qualifying transactions are those in which the merchant, acquirer, and issuer are in the same defined area. Also, the transaction currency is the local currency for that defined area for the transaction to qualify.

Visa also offers intraday settlement for countries with an NNSS or ANSS. Intraday settlement supports multiple settlement windows and facilitates delivery of settlement reports, interchange clearing files, and funds transfer instructions multiple times a day.
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) provides a variety of capabilities to clients.

Settlement relationships – VSS provides flexibility when defining settlement relationships. Clients can define from two to eight levels of settlement relationships. The different levels allow them to build and maintain the most appropriate settlement relationships for their business needs. For example, the settlement relationship levels can be used to reflect the products in a client's organization. As such, clients can easily and efficiently manage settlement functions. Report layouts and formats – VSS reports provide a common layout for BASE II- and SMS-cleared clients, allowing them to streamline their internal procedures. All VSS reports are available in print-ready and machine-readable formats. VSS reports use business-oriented terminology to better reflect the business needs of clients. Report delivery options – Clients can have their reports sent to multiple locations, including locations other than their processing centers. Interchange routing does not determine the routing of settlement information. Funds transfer points – The funds transfer point can be defined at any level in the settlement structure. This flexibility allows clients using third-party processors to be responsible for their own funds transfer.

Alternately routed and split-routed transactions – Clients can use an alternate processor, such as Visa Exceptions, to collect and deliver (switching) selected transactions. This option is called alternate routing for SMS and split routing for BASE II. Clients can also specify how they want to settle their alternately routed or split-routed transactions, electing to settle these transactions with their normally routed transactions or separately. National Settlement cutoff time – National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) or Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS) clients have the option to settle domestic activity at a time that is appropriate to their business day. The specific settlement time can be different from the International Settlement Service cutoff time. To use this feature, all clients participating in a particular NNSS or ANSS must agree on a common settlement cutoff time.
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) provides flexibility to clients through settlement reporting entities (SREs) and settlement hierarchies.
Clients need to consider certain rules when establishing settlement reporting entities (SREs) and settlement hierarchies.

Every client must participate in the International Settlement Service. An SRE must be established for every clearing entity in an International Settlement Service settlement hierarchy. A lowest-level SRE must be established for each clearing entity (acquiring or issuing identifier or card range in BASE II and affiliate ID in SMS). All SREs within a settlement hierarchy must use the same settlement currency. Every client has the option to participate in a National Net and Area Net Settlement Service if they are available in the client's region.

Separate settlement hierarchies with different SRE identifiers must be established for each settlement service. Settlement reporting for International Settlement Service transactions and National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) or Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS) transactions cannot be consolidated. Every clearing entity must be associated with a funds transfer point. The funds transfer point can be either the lowest-level SRE or a summary-level SRE. Each clearing entity can be associated with only one funds transfer point within a single hierarchy. An SRE can have only one summary-level SRE at the level above it. A summary-level SRE summarizes settlement information for all SREs linked to it in the settlement hierarchy.

A Settlement Reporting Entity (SRE) represents any business entity for which Visa performs settlement, provides settlement reporting, or both. Settlement reporting is available for every SRE. An SRE is identified by a unique 10-digit number that is assigned by Visa. An SRE can represent a processing center, client, or any segment of a client's business. For example:

Card product Issuer or acquirer business type Account ranges A combination of business entities or a summary of other SREs Funds transfer point Exception transactions Network affiliation, such as Plus or Visa
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) maintains this information for every SRE in a hierarchy:
SRE number SRE name Reporting options
VSS reports selected Report formats Delivery endpoints
Settlement Reporting Entity (SRE) types are used to construct a VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) hierarchy.

Lowest-level SRE – The lowest level at which VSS produces settlement reports. A lowest-level SRE can be associated with a clearing identifier, an account range, or, for SMS, with an affiliate ID plus a network. Summary-level SRE – A consolidation of lower-level SREs directly linked to a summary- level SRE through the settlement hierarchy. Top SRE – Mandatory for each hierarchy and includes a set of parameters that applies to the entire hierarchy, such as the settlement currency information. Funds Transfer SRE – The SRE or SREs where funds transfers (movement of funds) take place.

A lowest-level settlement reporting entity (SRE) can be associated with a clearing identifier, an account range, or, for SMS, with an affiliate ID plus a network. These terms help define a lowest-level SRE:

Clearing Entity – The entity used by the clearing systems to determine processing rules. In BASE II, a clearing entity is a 6-digit, Visa-assigned acquiring or issuing identifier or an International Organization for Standardization (ISO)-assigned card range. In the Single Message System (SMS), a clearing entity is the 6-digit, Visa-assigned acquiring or issuing identifier, which is the first six digits of the affiliate ID. The clearing entity is always included in the definition of a lowest-level SRE. Network – For Visa and VisaNet, the network is the telecommunications facility used for message switching. For other card program networks (for example, Plus and Interlink), the network dictates the product rules under which a transaction is processed. Settlement Service – A settlement service directs transactions through either the Visa International Settlement Service (the most commonly used settlement service) or through a National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) or Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS). An NNSS or ANSS is used by participating countries to settle domestic transactions when the issuer, acquirer, and merchant are in the same location. Every client must participate in the International Settlement Service and can also participate in an NNSS or ANSS to which they qualify. The settlement service identifier is always included as part of the definition of a lowest-level SRE. All SREs within a settlement hierarchy must be for the same settlement service.

Processor – A processor is a Visa endpoint that submits transactions to, or receives transactions from, SMS or BASE II. This endpoint is also referred to as a client processing center. The processor is always included in the definition of a lowest-level SRE and is used to differentiate transactions when a client uses multiple processors for processing its transactions. An example is when original transactions are processed through one processor, and exception transactions are processed by Visa Exceptions. Transaction Currency – When a transaction currency is included to define a lowest- level SRE, clients can settle in different currencies without a new acquiring or issuing identifier. Transactions in currencies that are not specified in an SRE will be settled in the primary settlement currency of the client. Therefore, the client need not define a lowest-level SRE for all transaction currencies. This option applies to the International Settlement Service only.
These examples show how lowest-level SREs are defined in certain situations.

When an SMS-connected client does not participate in an NNSS, the lowest-level SRE is defined by the affiliate ID (which is a combination of the clearing entity and network), the processor, and the International Settlement Service. When a BASE II-connected client does not participate in an NNSS, the lowest-level SRE is defined by the clearing entity, the processor, and the International Settlement Service. When a client participates in an NNSS, two lowest-level SREs must be established for each acquiring or issuing identifier. One SRE, for the NNSS, is defined by the clearing entity, the network (SMS only), the processor, and the NNSS. The other SRE, for the International Settlement Service, is defined by the clearing entity, the network (SMS only), the processor, and the International Settlement Service. When a client has work processed by two different processors, two lowest-level SREs must be established. Both SREs are defined by the clearing entity, the network (SMS only), the processor, and the settlement service. An example of a client with work processed by two processors is a client that uses a third-party processor to handle its original interchange and its own processing center to handle its back-office transactions. An issuing client that wants to report by account type, brand, cardholder type, or by a co-branding relationship must be set up as a lowest-level SRE, with the corresponding card range as the clearing entity. SMS clients must establish a clearing entity ID that corresponds to the card range.

A summary-level settlement reporting entity (SRE) is used to summarize reporting or funds transfer activity for the subordinate SREs below the summary-level SRE. In a two-level hierarchy, the summary-level SRE is the top SRE. A summary-level SRE is not associated with a clearing identifier, account range, or SMS affiliate ID plus a network, nor does it contain any parameters that apply to the entire hierarchy. A summary-level SRE can be established as a funds transfer point for all of the SREs below it. In addition, summary reports can be subscribed to the summary-level SRE that includes summarized activity for all of the SREs below the summary-level SRE.

A top settlement reporting entity (SRE) is a summary-level SRE that includes a set of parameters that apply to the entire hierarchy. For example, the top SRE includes the settlement currency used to settle all transactions that are processed in the hierarchy. There is only one top SRE in a hierarchy. Every hierarchy must have a top SRE. A top SRE can function as a summary-level SRE and funds transfer point, regardless of the number of levels included in the hierarchy. A top SRE only has SREs below it, not above it.

Funds transfer can occur at any level of the hierarchy: lowest level, summary level, or at the top level of the hierarchy. When a Settlement Reporting Entity (SRE) is established as a funds transfer point, the SRE is often called the Funds Transfer SRE (FTSRE). There is no limit to the number of FTSREs in a hierarchy, which depends on the number of levels in the hierarchy and the business requirements. The structure of funds transfers within a hierarchy must follow one rule: a funds transfer SRE cannot be directly linked to another funds transfer SRE, either above it or below it.

Settlement Reporting Entities (SREs) are linked together to form a structure called a settlement hierarchy. A diagram of the hierarchy is created in a vertical pattern to illustrate how one level connects to (rolls up to) the level above or below it. Understanding the connection between levels is important when determining the location of funds transfer SREs and report subscriptions. A settlement hierarchy is designed by a client to support the client's business needs. Clients have the option to have one or more settlement hierarchies, depending on their business requirements. A basic hierarchy must include at least two of these levels:
One top SRE One or more lowest-level SREs At least one funds transfer SRE

Note: The exception to the requirements for a basic hierarchy is a hierarchy for a Copy Request Manager (CRM). These hierarchies are a single level, do not require an FTSRE, and are used for exception item processing. There are two types of hierarchies: standard and customized.

The standard settlement hierarchy is a two-level settlement structure, with the funds transfer point at either the highest or lowest level. SREs are linked together to form a structure called a settlement hierarchy. Standard settlement hierarchies can be customized at any time after they are established to better support client business.

The standard hierarchy for Single Message System (SMS)-connected settlement is a two-level settlement hierarchy. The lowest level is defined by settlement service, affiliate ID (the 6-digit, Visa-assigned acquiring or issuing identifier and the 4-digit network identifier), and processor. Lowest-level SREs are consolidated into a summary-level SRE, which represents the processor and funds transfer point. Standard Settlement Hierarchy – SMS Client

If a client uses SMS routing options, a separate settlement hierarchy is established for each processor, which must include a separate funds transfer for each hierarchy. To consolidate the funds transfers, a custom hierarchy must be used to combine the two hierarchies into one with one funds transfer.

The standard hierarchy for BASE II-connected settlement is a two-level settlement hierarchy. The lowest-level SREs are consolidated to a top-level SRE, which represents the processor. Funds transfer occurs at either the top-level SRE or lowest-level SRE. The figure shows the standard BASE II settlement hierarchy.
Standard Settlement Hierarchy – BASE II Client

When a client participates in a National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) or an Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS), separate settlement hierarchies are established: one for the International Settlement Service and one for the NNSS or ANSS. In a standard NNSS hierarchy, the funds transfer point can be either at the top level or at the lowest level. This example shows the standard hierarchy established for each settlement service.

The standard settlement hierarchies for the two settlement services are structured the same, but they have two separate sets of settlement reporting entities (SREs). The funds transfers for the International Settlement Service and NNSS are reported separately. The funds transfer for the International Settlement Service is at the top level. The funds transfer for the NNSS is at the lowest level. In the NNSS, all acquiring or issuing identifiers for this processor settle at the acquiring or issuing identifier level.
Standard Settlement Hierarchy for Each Settlement Service
In this example, all acquiring or issuing identifiers participate in the NNSS.

A custom hierarchy is one that has between three and eight levels. In general, a multilevel hierarchy is used to include summary-level points for reporting and funds transfer, represented by a summary-level settlement reporting entity (SRE). A summary-level SRE can be the designated SRE wherever a client wishes to have reporting or funds transfer for the SREs at levels below the summary-level SRE. If a client wants to establish a customized settlement hierarchy, these objectives can be met:

Client settlement across processors—A client using multiple processors consolidates its funds transfer. Combined BASE II and SMS settlement activity. Additional lower-level reporting. Different settlement structures for International Settlement Service and National Net Settlement Service.
The different types of hierarchies are designed to provide settlement reporting and funds transfers for specific client requirements.

Standard client-level settlement Customized client-level settlement Client settlement across processors Combined BASE II- and SMS-connected activity Additional lower-level reporting International and National Net Settlement Services

VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) can accommodate clients that use processors but want to handle their own funds transfer. A funds transfer settlement reporting entity (FTSRE) can be defined at any level within a hierarchy. In this example, the processor is represented by settlement reporting entity (SRE) 4 and the clients behind the processor by SRE 1, 2, and 3. Funds transfers are located at SRE 1, 2, and 3. These SREs subscribe to detail-level reporting. SRE 4 does not need to perform funds transfer, and subscribes to processor-level reporting.
In some cases, the processor can be the funds transfer point for some of its clients, while other clients act as their own funds transfer points. This example illustrates the hierarchy.
Customized Settlement Hierarchy – Combining Client and Processor Settlement

Bank A has its own funds transfer, while funds transfer for banks B and C is performed by the processor. A summary-level settlmenet reporting entity (SRE) (SRE 5) is defined as the funds transfer SRE for banks B and C. All three banks use Processor A to send and receive transactions to and from VisaNet. To receive settlement reports for all three banks, Processor A is defined with an SRE in the settlement hierarchy. SRE 1 represents the client-level funds transfer for Bank A, and SRE 5 represents the funds transfer for banks B and C.

Through VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS), a bank that uses multiple processors can receive a single funds transfer. In this example, when a client establishes the standard settlement hierarchy structure the client processors can no longer be included in a settlement hierarchy that represents all of their work.
Standard Settlement Hierarchy – Client Settlement Across Processors

The flexibility to define funds transfer points and reporting levels within VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) also allows consolidation of funds transfer activity and settlement reporting for SMS affiliate IDs and clearing identifiers. Standard Settlement Hierarchy – Combined BASE II- and SMS-Connected Activity

The settlement reports requested for settlement reporting entity (SRE) 5 provide SMS and BASE II consolidated information. Settlement reports requested for SRE 1 provide BASE II-connected settlement information. Settlement reports requested for SREs 2, 3, and 4 provide SMS- connected settlement information for Visa, Plus, and Interlink transactions, respectively. SRE 5 is defined as the funds transfer SRE.

In some cases, clients may want to receive settlement reports that include information at a lower level of detail. A multilevel settlement hierarchy enables clients to define multiple tiers of settlement reporting. This allows reporting based on a subset of a processor's or client's activity. Factors, including settlement reporting, can be defined by:
Issuer or acquirer business mode Processor
BASE II or SMS Clearing System Product

In this example, Bank C wants to receive separate settlement reports for Visa commercial card transactions and Visa consumer card transactions. Two additional, lower-level settlement reporting entities (SREs) must be established under SRE 3 (Bank C), one for each cardholder type. Customized Settlement Hierarchy – Additional Lower-Level Reporting

VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) clients have the option to establish an international hierarchy in one configuration and the National Net Settlement Service (NNSS), or Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS) hierarchy, in a different configuration. When the processor wants to receive additional levels of reporting within the International Settlement Service and wants to perform funds transfer for some of its acquiring or issuing identifiers in the NNSS or ANSS, the processor can establish the hierarchies. Customized Settlement Hierarchy – Summary-Level With Funds Transfer at Top Level
Customized NNSS Hierarchy – Summary-Level and Client-Level Settlement

The Multicurrency Settlement Service is an optional international service that allows clients that transact in multiple currencies to settle in more than one currency using a single acquiring or issuing identifier. Multicurrency Settlement can be established for acquiring and issuing identifiers and for clearing identifiers and SMS affiliate IDs. Through the Multicurrency Settlement Service, the same acquiring or issuing identifier used to establish a client's primary hierarchy can be used to establish one or more multicurrency hierarchies. Each multicurrency hierarchy includes a settlement currency that can be different from the settlement currency of the primary hierarchy. A lowest-level SRE is established in the multicurrency hierarchy with a transaction currency code that matches its settlement currency for either acquirer or issuer transactions. When a transaction originates in a currency that matches the transaction currency of the lowest-level SRE, the transaction is settled through the multicurrency hierarchy and currency conversion is not required.

This diagram of a primary hierarchy has a settlement currency of Euros. All non-Euro transactions processed through the primary hierarchy are converted to Euros and settled in Euros. In this example, the client wants all transactions that originate in British Pound Sterling (GBP) to settle in GBP. A second hierarchy is established to settle in GBP (SRE). The same acquiring or issuing identifier is used to create the primary hierarchy and the multicurrency hierarchy. Transactions from the acquiring or issuing identifier that originate in GBP are settled through the multicurrency hierarchy in GBP. Clients have the option to use the same acquiring or issuing identifier to establish a hierarchy for each Visa-authorized settlement currency that supports the client.

To reconcile VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports to clearing system reports, Visa recommends that SMS-connected clients establish a settlement reporting entity (SRE) that represents the affiliate ID (and processor, if more than one processor is used), and that BASE II- connected clients establish an SRE that represents the acquiring or issuing identifier. This SRE can be established at the lowest level or the summary level.

VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) supports settlement reporting for Single Message System (SMS)- and BASE II-connected clients by producing reports with standardized layouts.
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) uses various categories to create reports. These categories are identified as:
Business Mode Charge Type Business Transaction Type Business Transaction Cycle Jurisdiction
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports are divided into sections based on business mode. The business mode designates whether the amounts reported are for:
Note: The business mode Other contains all transactions that are not issuer or acquirer. These include fee collection and funds disbursement transactions.
Charge type is a way to classify charges on VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports.
BASE II processing charges International Acquiring Fee International Service Assessment (ISA) International Service Assessment Allocation Special Airline Fees (SAF) Returned item charges
See VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) User Guide, Volume 2, Reports.

To support consistent settlement reporting and make the reports more business-oriented, VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) business transaction types are used to classify transactions by their business purpose. In the clearing process, BASE II uses transaction codes and SMS uses message types to differentiate transactions. For example, in BASE II, the transaction code TC 05 is used for a purchase transaction, while in SMS, the message type 0200 is used. In VSS, the business transaction type is purchase for both a TC05 and a message type 0200. On VSS reports, transactions that represent different business transaction types are reported separately, such as purchase and quasi-cash transactions. See VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) User Guide, Volume 2, Reports.

The business transaction cycle further qualifies business transaction types to identify which presentment is being reported. For example, a purchase transaction presented for the first time by an acquirer has a cycle description of ORIGINAL. If it is sent back by the issuer, the cycle description is DISPUTE FIN for Visa disputes or CHARGEBACK for non-Visa disputes. If resubmitted by the acquirer, the cycle description is DISPUTE RESP FIN for Visa disputes or REPRESENTMENT for non-Visa disputes. Any of these presentments can be reversed. A reversal is indicated on the report by RVRSL next to the business transaction.

Jurisdiction identifies the operating regulations governing the reimbursement fees and charges imposed on a transaction. Examples of jurisdiction are Visa International, Visa Canada, Plus System, Inc. U.S.A, and Interlink International.

All VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports are available in machine-readable (TC 46) and print- ready (TC 47) formats. Reports can be delivered in either or both formats. A different format option can be selected for each report for the same settlement reporting entity (SRE). For example, some reports can be delivered in machine-readable format, some reports can be delivered in print-ready format, and still other reports can be delivered in both formats. The same report can be sent to separate locations in the same or different formats. Clients can take advantage of the machine-readable reports in a number of ways, including:

Producing customized settlement reports. Providing automated interfaces to internal processing systems. (For example, automated procedures can be developed for general ledger posting of reimbursement fees or Visa charges). Automating reconciliation procedures.
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reporting offers clients a variety of features.

Reporting is available for every settlement reporting entity (SRE) in the settlement hierarchy. Reports showing multicurrency transactions include subtotals by currency and the date of the currency rate table used so clients can reconcile settlement amounts to clearing amounts. Settlement amounts are reported in the minor units of currency appropriate to the settlement currency. For example, Japanese yen is reported as 100 and Canadian dollars as 100.00. Issuers are able to receive reconciliation information for International Service Assessment (ISA) and for optional issuer ISA fees. Optional issuer ISA is currently supported only by certain regions. Interchange amounts, reimbursement fees, and Visa charges settled by VSS are summarized on one report. Most settlement reports are available on a monthly basis. Fees and charges reports include a jurisdiction name that specifies the operating regulations, such as Visa International or Visa Canada, that govern reimbursement fees and charges for a transaction. Clients can use this information to help with reconciliation. All VSS reports are also available in machine-readable (TC 46) formats. This eliminates the need for clients to extract data fields from print-ready (TC 47) reports. Clients can have settlement reports sent to multiple locations of their choice. All VSS National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) or Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS) reports have the same name and format as their international counterparts. Clients that participate in an NNSS receive two sets of VSS reports: one set that shows transactions, fees, and charges settled through the International Settlement Service, and another that shows transactions, fees, and charges settled through the NNSS. The settlement service identifier appears in the report heading. VSS reports are produced and delivered seven days a week. Any SRE participating in the International Settlement Service receives null reports when there is no activity during a reporting period. This feature is not available for NNSS reports.
Reimbursement fees and Visa charges are reported on VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports.

Reimbursement fees are amounts paid by one client to another client for transactions entered into interchange. Visa charges include all amounts that are assessed by Visa and paid by the client or the client processor to Visa. This category also includes amounts paid by Visa to the client or client processor.

Monthly fees and charges settlement are supported in VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS). Clients' fees and charges-pending reports are available for subscription, VSS–610 and VSS–640. The monthly fees and charges settlement use the existing defer-settlement process. The clearing system calculates fees and charges daily with a future settlement date (the last calendar date of the month) and settlement warehouses the future-dated fees and charges in a “defer” file until the settlement date.
Fees and charges are grouped by categories on VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports.

Business mode – Designates whether the amounts reported are for issuer, acquirer, or other. Charge type – Provides a means of classifying charges on the VSS reports. Business transaction type – Classifies transactions according to their business purpose. Jurisdiction – Identifies the Operating Regulations that govern the reimbursement fees and charges imposed on a transaction. Transaction routing – Describes the source and destination of the transaction. When the transaction is interregional, the routing indicates the source and destination regions. When the routing is intraregional, the reports show the source and destination countries. Fee level – Indicates the type of fee assessed.
Interchange Reimbursement Fees (IRFs) are noninterchange amounts paid by one client to another client. Reimbursement fees are reported on these reports:
VSS–130 – Reimbursement Fees Report VSS–130–M – Monthly Reimbursement Fees Report VSS–135 – Month-to-Date Reimbursement Fees Report

blocks.text: VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) testing is available for clients that are BASE II- and Single Message System (SMS)-connected through the VisaNet Certification Management System (VCMS). Testing is available for clients preparing for a VSS implementation or modifying their existing VSS hierarchies or report subscriptions. Testing also supports BASE II- and SMS-clearing services. VCMS can generate VSS reports and files from controlled sets of test data. VCMS can also be used to test and certify SMS messages. During VSS testing with VisaNet, the client is responsible for validating test results and ensuring that the VSS reports and files can be processed correctly. Certain products or services may require certification with Visa. Certification covers the evaluation of online message formats, including the 0520 reconciliation message and the 0620 funds transfer totals message, and does not imply that Visa has certified a client's overall system or processes. During client certification with VisaNet, a Visa representative ensures that Visa conducts checks for selective output results from a specifically defined client test.
Testing enables clients to receive files and reports that can be used to test their internal systems and procedures. VSS testing enables clients to:

Review the VSS reports and files before implementation or change of settlement hierarchies or reporting options. Ensure that internal systems and procedures have been appropriately developed. Use the reports and output from internal systems as a basis for staff training. Review the impact of the SMS reports and VisaNet Integrated Payment (V.I.P.) System raw data on internal systems, such as space allocation and transmission times (SMS clients only).
Clients can also use the VSS test output to verify software upgrades for these VSS features:
VSS reports as print-ready (TC 47) format, machine-readable (TC 46) format, or both formats SMS raw data (SMS only) SMS reports (SMS only) Automated reconciliation
Note: Clients can combine VSS testing with any other product or service testing.
VSS Test Report and File Delivery
All test output is delivered using production report delivery methods. Existing clients are responsible for keeping test output separate from production output.

Clients using BASE II- and SMS-clearing can have all test output delivered to a VisaNet Access Point (VAP). Report and test files are identified by the word TEST in the header record (TC 90). Clients can receive VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) report data in machine-readable (TC 46) format, print-ready (TC 47) format, or both formats. SMS detail reports are received in general delivery reports (TC 45) format or raw data multipurpose message (TC 33) format.

Clients in the U.S. region using SMS clearing can use a non-VAP delivery method to receive test output. However, a non-VAP delivery of test output requires a manual process. A Visa representative coordinates non-VAP deliveries with Visa Operations and the client.
When developing a test plan, VisaNet Settlement Services (VSS) clients consider various factors by completing certain tasks. These tasks must be completed before beginning testing:

Determine the VSS hierarchy and VSS report options. Determine the SMS report options and V.I.P. raw data options (SMS only). Determine funds transfer point. Determine testing schedule with a Visa representative. Develop all internal processes (manual and automated) that use settlement reports. Develop processes that use V.I.P. raw data (optional, SMS only). Develop or modify systems, as required, to accommodate machine-readable (TC 46) formats (optional). Develop systems as required to process 0520 reconciliation and 0620 funds transfer totals messages (optional, SMS only).
Note: Clients receiving the 0520 reconciliation message or the 0620 funds transfer totals message for the first time must certify.

Plan training to familiarize staff with the layouts and terminology used in the settlement reports. Plan training so staff can use the VSS and SMS reports for reconciliation and other downstream processes. Clients that want to test a customized VSS hierarchy may need additional testing setup lead time. Custom hierarchies can require three (3) weeks to set up. Clients should contact their Visa representative for assistance in determining the exact amount of time required. Clients must allow sufficient time to review reports and incorporate the test results as part of their planned reconciliation and training processes.

Each settlement service (National Net Settlement Service or International) requires a separate settlement hierarchy. Clients can elect to schedule a test for each settlement hierarchy separately. Clients must plan for sufficient disk space to receive the test files and reports.

Client testing is performed using VisaNet Certification Management Service (VCMS). Clients can submit and receive controlled sets of test data and reports through VCMS. VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) and Single Message System (SMS) reports and files are generated according to the VSS configuration defined for the test. VCMS testing is available to new and existing clients. Existing clients can test changes to their settlement hierarchy and reporting options.
VisaNet Certification Management Service (VCMS) testing provides specific benefits to clients. VCMS enables clients to:

Conduct tests on a daily basis during the week and, in some regions, also on Saturday. Confirm VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) report balances using controlled test data. Develop internal reconciliation procedures using the test output. Confirm hierarchies, established by initial setups or changes to existing setups, using controlled test data and selected test account numbers. Conduct certification of 0520 reconciliation messages and 0620 funds transfer totals messages.

VisaNet Certification Management Service (VCMS) testing is available 7 days a week, Monday through Sunday, for all regions. One set of VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports per settlement service is generated daily. A Start and End date must be specified for the test. The VSS test configuration is set up in VCMS for the dates specified. The test configuration is not maintained after the end date specified, unless a request to change the date is submitted. Null VSS reports are generated on days when no test data is submitted. No SMS reports are produced on those days. Clients preparing to test using the VCMS service must indicate the test start and end date to their Visa representative.

Because of the lead-time required for setup, clients requiring custom hierarchies should contact their Visa representative well in advance of the requested test dates. A test with a custom hierarchy can require up to 3 weeks setup time. Your Visa representative assists in determining the amount of lead time that is required for a test with a custom hierarchy. Note: Requested changes to the test VSS hierarchy or report delivery options (such as adding an acquiring or issuing identifier or adding a report) are effective on the second Monday after the request.
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) clients using BASE II Clearing can perform testing using VisaNet Certification Management Service (VCMS).

BASE II clients can submit and receive test transactions and select test account numbers. BASE II-connected acquirers can generate a maximum of 3,000 test transactions per day. BASE II-connected issuers can receive data for any or all of the services that are currently supported in the VisaNet Certification Management Service (VCMS) environment. A Visa representative sets up testing data. One settlement cycle is run each day. Test output includes interchange files, VSS reports, and Edit Package reports. Testing is available on central processing dates (CPDs) 7 days a week, Monday through Sunday, for all regions. Custom implementations, changes to existing hierarchies, and reporting options may require more setup lead-time depending on the complexity of the customization. Clients should contact their Visa representative for assistance in determining lead-time requirements for setting up their test. Clients must request testing three (3) weeks before the Monday of the week they want testing to begin. Clients must provide their Visa representative the specific information to schedule a VCMS test:

VSS report selection and choice of formats: machine-readable (TC 46), print-ready (TC 47), or both formats. Each processor (CIB) and its corresponding client name. The Monday date of the week testing is to start. Testing is available on the Monday of the start week, but clients can begin testing any day of the week. Clients receive VSS null reports on days when no tests are performed. Report and file delivery information. The date testing is to end. Any hierarchy or reporting option changes to existing VSS hierarchies.
BASE II Report and File Delivery

The VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports are delivered to the Visa Access Point (VAP) as test files between 0330 and 0430 Greenwich mean time (GMT) every day a test is scheduled. The VSS reports and files are delivered to the client's VAP with TEST displayed in the header. Clients can differentiate test reports and files from production reports and files by checking for TEST in the header.

VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) clients using Single Message System (SMS) clearing can test using VisaNet Certification Management Service (VCMS). Testing begins by executing an online test. The test data is used with the test VSS hierarchy to create VSS reports, SMS reports, and raw data. Visa can provide SMS certification scripts to clients for testing. Testing is available 7 days a week, Monday through Sunday, for all regions. SMS-connected clients run controlled sets of test data and should review the results in the next day's reporting cycle using these outputs: VSS settlement reports, SMS reports, and SMS raw data.

Single Message System (SMS)-connected clients must certify when first implementing SMS processing. VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) clients who elect to receive the 0520 reconciliation message or the 0620 funds transfer totals message for the first time must also certify.

A Visa representative sets up test data for Single Message System (SMS)-connected clients with VisaNet Certification Management Service (VCMS). Clients can submit and receive test transactions and select test account numbers. One settlement cycle is run each day. Clients can receive data for any or all of the services that are currently supported in the VCMS environment. Custom implementations and significant changes to existing settlement hierarchies and reporting options may require more setup lead-time depending on the complexity of the customization. Clients should contact their Visa representative for assistance in determining lead-time requirements for setting up their test environment. Clients must request testing a minimum of three (3) weeks before the Monday of the week testing begins. Clients must provide their Visa representative specific information to schedule a test:

VSS report selection and choice of VSS report formats: machine-readable (TC 46), print- ready (TC 47), or both formats. Identification of hierarchy structure summary levels and funds transfer points. SMS report selection, SMS report sort order, and SMS report lines.

Selection of V.I.P. raw data records. Choice of 0520 reconciliation and 0620 funds transfer totals messages. Each affiliate ID and processor to be tested. The Monday date that the testing is to start. Testing becomes available on the Monday of the start week, but clients can begin testing any day of the week. Clients receive VSS null reports on days when no tests are performed. The date testing is to end. Report and file delivery information.
Note: If additional testing time is required after an established end date, clients should contact their Visa representative to ensure successful results.

For VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) clients using Visa Access Point (VAP) delivery, reports and raw data are delivered to the client's VAP within 24 to 32 hours after a test. The VSS reports and files are delivered to the client's VAP with TEST displayed in the header. Clients can differentiate test reports and files from production reports and files by checking for TEST in the header. Clients in the U.S. region using a non-VAP delivery method should have their Visa representative coordinate the test output delivery. Test output can only be generated once each day that a test is scheduled.

This list contains suggestions for using the test output and is not a comprehensive list. Clients are responsible for determining which steps are necessary to ensure that their systems and procedures are ready for implementing VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) or for changing their current setup.

Use VSS output to familiarize staff with the layouts and terminology used in the settlement reports. Test internal procedures. Confirm VSS report balances using controlled quantities of selected test data. Verify VSS and SMS report selections. Confirm acquiring or issuing identifier selection, hierarchy, and other VSS options for reporting and funds transfer. Determine whether business objectives were achieved and data is being reported as needed.
The VSS test output can also be used to test clients' internal systems:

Receipt and use of machine-readable (TC 46) report format (optional). Receipt and use of V.I.P. raw data (optional, SMS only). Automated reconciliation procedures. Receipt of SMS 0520 reconciliation messages. Receipt of these messages is optional. Clients receiving these messages for the first time must certify (SMS only). Receipt of SMS 0620 funds transfer totals message. Receipt of this message is optional. SMS clients receiving the 0620 funds transfer totals message for the first time must certify (SMS only).

Prior to implementation, clients and processors must consider various internal factors to determine the requirements for successful VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) implementation. Visa provides various worksheets for recording clients’ implementation decisions to aid in the planning process.

Clients use various worksheets to record their VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) implementation plans. These worksheets are used to communicate client VSS implementation requirements to a Visa representative.
Used to record decisions regarding basic internal implementation requirements and the implementation date.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding funds transfer processing.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding hierarchy options.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding the VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reporting options.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding VSS report options for BASE II-connected clients.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding VSS report options for Single Message System (SMS)- connected clients.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding SMS options.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding SMS report options for SMS-connected clients.
Used to record implementation decisions regarding VSS testing.
VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) hierarchy implementation can be done using a standard or a custom method. Clients must determine which implementation strategy to use.

Standard – This implementation type creates a two-level hierarchy, with one top settlement reporting entity (SRE) that includes parameters that define the entire hierarchy, such as the settlement currency code. The top SRE also represents a summary of all SREs below the top SRE. In a standard hierarchy, the top SRE represents all activity cleared (processed) by the processor. The lowest-level SREs are either identifiers (acquirers and issuers) or account ranges (issuers). Funds transfer can occur at the top level or at the lowest level (client-level settlement). Reporting options for a standard hierarchy can be defined by groups of acquiring or issuing identifiers or can apply to all SREs within the hierarchy. Multiple report delivery destinations must be requested as a custom implementation. Custom – Customizing a standard hierarchy may be needed for many reasons including:

Using midlevel summary reporting Establishing additional funds transfer points Sending reports to additional endpoints Creating a VSS hierarchy that involves acquiring or issuing identifiers clearing through multiple processors
Record the implementation method information in the Internal Plans – All Clients Worksheet.

The VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) standard settlement hierarchy is determined by identifying every clearing identifier associated with a processor and establishing a two-level hierarchy setup. Standard hierarchies are constructed based on how transactions are cleared in BASE II or SMS. Lowest-level SREs are defined by:
Acquiring or issuing identifiers or account ranges for BASE II Affiliate IDs in SMS

Reporting and optional funds transfer for the lowest-level settlement reporting entity (SRE) is consolidated, at the processor level, to one top-level SRE. A standard implementation of clients with only one acquiring or issuing identifier results in a standard hierarchy that consists of two SREs: a highest-level funds transfer SRE and a lowest- level SRE that represents the acquiring or issuing identifier. Totals on the reports for both SREs are the same. To eliminate duplicate reports for the two SREs, reporting can be subscribed at the top level only. However, if client-level funds transfer is supported, each lowest-level SRE must subscribe to the VSS–110 report.

In a standard hierarchy, funds transfer can take place at the highest-level settlement reporting entity (SRE) or at the lowest level. The funds transfer point must have a settlement account established at the settlement bank of the client's choice. The settlement account must be open and funded by the implementation date. National Net and Area Net Settlement hierarchies can also have the funds transfer points at the top level or lowest level.

VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) clients can choose these VSS reporting options with a standard implementation of VSS. Reporting options can be defined by groups of acquiring or issuing identifiers, or can apply to all settlement reporting entities (SREs) within the hierarchy. (Multiple report delivery destinations must be requested as a custom implementation.)
VSS settlement report selection Report format Acquiring or issuing identifier identification in report data records

All settlment reporting entities (SREs) in a VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) hierarchy must have the same settlement currency. Because National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) and Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS) hierarchies are separate from International Settlement hierarchies, an NNSS or ANSS currency may be a different currency from the one used for International Settlement.

Clients can customize their settlement structures by defining more than two reporting levels, or choosing different reporting options for each settlement reporting entity (SRE) in the VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS).

A custom VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) implementation is required when a standard implementation does not meet the client's settlement or reporting needs. A custom implementation is necessary to support these business needs:

Providing additional funds transfer levels. Providing business-related settlement hierarchies instead of a processing-defined hierarchy. Delivering reports to multiple locations. Receiving additional summary reporting levels.

Clients have the option to include one or more summary-level settlement reporting entities (SREs) in a customized hierarchy. Summary-level SREs can be used in a hierarchy to summarize reporting or funds transfer for the SREs below the summary-level SRE. When a client creates a new hierarchy or customizes an existing hierarchy, it is suggested that the lowest-level SREs be established first. Once the client understands the function of each lowest-level SRE, it is easier to determine how summary-level SREs can be included to group lower-level SREs for either reporting or funds transfer purposes, or for both reporting and funds transfer.

Clients have the option of establishing multiple funds transfer at multiple levels within a single VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) hierarchy. Multiple funds transfers can be included to support the client business as defined by the hierarchy. Each funds transfer point must have a funded settlement account established at the settlement bank of the client's choice by the implementation date.

VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) clients can customize the way VSS reporting options are implemented. Reporting options can be different for each settlement reporting entity (SRE) or group of SREs in a hierarchy. These reporting options can be customized:

VSS settlement report selection Report format Report delivery to specified processor or client endpoint Report delivery to multiple endpoints Acquiring or issuing identifier identification in report data records BASE II clearing charges assessed at processor level

Certain areas of a client's environment must be evaluated when planning an implementation of VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS). These tasks must be completed to determine the impact of VSS on the client's internal processes:

Identification of all acquiring or issuing identifiers, including identification of acquiring or issuing identifiers participating in a National Net or Area Net Settlement Service, using SMS routing options, or BASE II split routing Determine processing requirements to support the delivery of files, including machine- readable format and V.I.P. raw data files Determine automated reconciliation processing Familiarize staff with the report layouts and terminology used in the VSS settlement reports Determine business and financial reporting requirements

Clients must also evaluate their testing needs to ensure that their systems are capable of receiving and processing the reports, report formats, and, when applicable, VisaNet Integrated Payment (V.I.P.) System raw data and SMS online messages.

Various support areas may need to be included to ensure a smooth implementation of VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS), and to ensure that current business processes are not interrupted. Although a formal project team may not be dedicated to the implementation tasks, these support areas should be considered:
Determine how VisaNet activity should be reported considering the VSS options. Create written procedures.
Create written procedures. Train appropriate staff to use the new procedures.

Determine how the VSS and SMS print-ready reports are to be produced and stored and the impacts of implementing machine-readable formats and V.I.P. raw data. Determine the impacts to possible downstream environments. Determine the impacts to automated file processing. Determine capacity requirements for system environments.
Evaluate funds transfer requirements. Complete the Treasury-related paperwork as provided by the Visa representative.
Record this support information in the Internal Plans – All Clients Worksheet:
Internal areas that will support VSS implementation. If all internal areas have been contacted.

The impact of VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) on a client's internal processes depends on the client's processing environment. The process environments depend upon processing and structural relationships, which can be structured based on business functions. Clients must plan the environmental tasks needed to successfully complete implementation.

Generally, clients have a settlement structure based on their processing structure. Under the VisaNet Settlement System (VSS), clients have the option of establishing settlement relationships independent of their processing relationships. This option must be coordinated with their processor. Consider these questions when evaluating processing relationships:
Is more than one processor used? If more than one processor is used, how is activity split among processors?
VSS Acquiring or Issuing Identifier Identification

At the time a hierarchy is set up in VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS), clients must provide identification of all acquiring or issuing identifiers to their Visa representative. Acquiring or issuing identifiers include:
Clearing identifiers SMS affiliate IDs, including network IDs.

If SMS affiliate IDs use routing options or Visa Exceptions, clients must identify all acquiring or issuing identifiers separately. If the acquiring or issuing identifiers are participating in a National Net Settlement Service, clients must identify which acquiring or issuing identifiers will be excluded, if any.
Record this acquiring or issuing identifier information in the Internal Plans – All Clients Worksheet:

Identify all acquiring or issuing identifiers. If more than one processor will be used. If Yes, determine how activity is split among processors. If transactions are cleared through BASE II, SMS, or both.

If transactions are to be cleared through BASE II, determine if BASE II exception activity is split to another processor. If transactions are to be cleared through SMS, determine which SMS routing options are used. Determine if this activity is included in the new hierarchy. For example: Original routing Alternate routing Account type routing ATM/POS routing PIN/No PIN routing If transactions are to be cleared through SMS, determine if this activity is included in the new hierarchy, for example, if Visa exceptions are used.
Clients must determine what type of settlement arrangements are required. Record this settlement information in the Internal Plans – All Clients Worksheet:

If the processor will serve as the settlement agent or if another business entity will be involved. If one or more National Net or Area Net Settlement Services will be used. One VisaNet Settlement System (VSS) hierarchy will be established for each settlement service. For a National Net or Area Net Settlement Service, if the settlement will occur at the processor or acquiring or issuing identifier level. All settlement currencies to be used. All SREs in a VSS hierarchy must use the same settlement currency. If multiple settlement currencies are used, a separate hierarchy is required for each settlement currency.

The reconciliation process and the level of automation of reconciliation procedures are two of the most significant planning decisions for implementing the VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS). Consider using:

Print-ready (TC 47) VSS settlement reports. SMS transaction detail reports. Machine-readable (TC 46) VSS settlement information for automated downloading of settlement information and other automated reconciliation procedures. SMS raw data by SMS clients to reconcile against transaction data stored in internal log files or download information to history files.
See VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) User Guide, Volume 2, Reports. Record this reconciliation procedure information in the Internal Plans – All Clients Worksheet:
The reconciliation procedures you developed. Which reconciliation procedures are automated. What to do with Visa Reports:
Load to an online system Archive Store on microfiche or other report viewing system
Which internal departments will use Visa reports and the information that is important to each.

The size and complexity of the client's hierarchy can contribute to the reporting volume. VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) reports are created by settlement reporting entity (SRE); therefore, the more SREs in the hierarchy, the more report lines. Other factors that can influence capacity needs include:
Size of hierarchy indicated by the number of SREs. Number of VSS reporting levels.

Number of VSS reports selected for each SRE. Delivery of VSS reports in both print-ready and machine-readable formats. SMS report size depends on volume of activity and numbers of report lines selected for each report or sort option of report. Null daily VSS reports are generated and sent for all SREs when there is no activity (International settlement only). When clients do not run the Edit Package on Sunday, the files on Monday might be large because they also include Sunday's reports. Receipt of V.I.P. Raw Data Release 2.2. The size of this file depends on the transaction volume and the selected record types.
Record this capacity information in the Internal Plans – All Clients Worksheet:
The capacity of the processing location. The potential impact various options may have on processing.
Clients must consider various services related to VisaNet Settlement Service (VSS) settlement hierarchies, regardless of the planned implementation type. Areas for consideration include:
National Net or Area Net Settlement Service Deferred Settlement Service Routing Options
Note: Deferred settlement is currently available only in Brazil, Japan, Argentina, and Chile.
Clients implementing a National Net Settlement Service (NNSS) or Area Net Settlement Service (ANSS) need a separate settlement hierarchy for each settlement service. Separate hierarchies
